evals.prompt: I run the affiliate program at Lumaflor, a DTC haircare brand. We approve around 400 affiliates a month - mostly coupon sites, a few Instagram creators, and some newsletter people. Right now the only thing they get is an approval email saying 'welcome, you're in.' My VA generates their tracking link and coupon code by hand and emails it over, usually 2 or 3 business days later. I want a proper welcome email series, and I'd like white-glove treatment: a personal call with each new affiliate in week one. I don't have anyone dedicated to the program, it's me plus the VA. Can you write me the sequence?
evals.expected_output: A sequence plan that first fixes day-0 provisioning and pins an activation definition, removes the requested per-affiliate call tier outright given no AM and 400 approvals a month, routes the whole intake self-serve with per-archetype first actions, and delivers the SEQUENCE PLAN artifact with a behavior-trigger layer.
expectations: Fixes the activation event and its measurement window (for example first tracked sale within 30 days of approval) before designing any touch
Flags the 2-3 business day manual link and code delivery as a day-0 provisioning failure that must be fixed before the sequence launches, not as a touch inside the sequence
Contrasts auto-provisioning at approval (affiliate ready to promote in under an hour) with manual provisioning taking 1-3 business days
Declines the requested personal call with every new affiliate
Removes the high-touch tier from the menu entirely rather than listing it as a lower-priority or later option
Justifies that removal by the absence of a named affiliate manager and the roughly 400 approvals per month volume
Routes the whole intake to a self-serve tier (portal plus automated drip) as the floor
States the tier efficiency ordering explicitly, with self-serve ahead of hybrid ahead of high-touch on activation bought per manager hour
Notes that self-serve leads on that ratio despite converting worst per affiliate, not because it converts best
Places the tracking link and coupon code in the first lines of touch 1
Keeps touch 1 to one action and roughly 300 words or fewer
Gives coupon-deal, social creator, and email-list owner archetypes different first actions and leading assets, without ranking those archetypes against each other
Delivers a SEQUENCE PLAN artifact carrying at least Activation, Routing, Touches, Activation nudge, Never-activated, Exits, and KPIs lines

evals.prompt: Our affiliate program shows 4% activation and my CMO is furious. Program's been live 8 months, roughly 90 approvals a month, B2C home goods. I've been told the welcome email is the problem - it's honestly pretty bland. Can you rewrite it and the two follow-ups? We're on a standard affiliate platform with cookie-based tracking only, no server-side postback. Affiliates do show clicks in the dashboard though.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rewrite copy first, replaced by an ordered diagnosis that starts with an end-to-end conversion trace (justified by clicks-visible / activation-low plus cookie-only tracking), then the approval-email check, per-touch engagement, cohort split and nudge/branch audit, with the rewrite placed last.
expectations: Refuses to rewrite the welcome email as the first action and says so explicitly
Gives the reason that a rewrite is a change rather than a check, and that it destroys the baseline that would have shown whether it worked
Starts with an end-to-end trace of one conversion: click, recorded conversion, pending commission, reversal state
Ties that first step to the stated symptom of clicks visible in the dashboard while activation reports low, as a sign the reported number may be fiction
States the diagnosis ordering as information bought per unit of effort rather than cheapest check first
Includes opening the approval email as a newly approved affiliate to confirm a working link or code is present, described as near-zero effort
Includes reading the per-touch open and click rates the platform already records, and notes this localizes where the sequence loses people without naming the cause
Includes splitting activation by archetype and by tier as a separate check
Includes auditing whether a deadline-bound nudge inside the window and a designed never-activated branch exist
Flags cookie-only attribution as undercounting because of browser tracking prevention, and recommends server-side postback carrying a click ID and an order or transaction ID
Places the rewrite of touch 1 or the asset kit last, only after the preceding checks have run
Does not conclude that recruitment or affiliate quality is the cause

evals.prompt: Draft the day-45 email for affiliates in our program who still haven't sent a single click. I want it firm - something like 'accounts with no activity within 60 days of approval will be removed from the program, so get your first link out now.' We're a B2C pet supplies store, 30-day activation window, and honestly the dead weight in the account list is making our numbers look terrible. Also tell me how many times to chase them and when I should just delete these accounts.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the termination-threat wording on motivation grounds, replaced with an opportunity-framed deadline incentive, plus a never-activated branch that diagnoses first, re-engages once or twice, sends a housekeeping-framed final notice at roughly six months, and archives rather than deletes.
expectations: Rejects the proposed removal-threat wording and does not produce a version of it
Gives the reason as motivation research finding threats counterproductive, rather than as a tone or brand preference
Reframes the message as an opportunity with a finish line, for example an incentive that expires on a stated date
Recommends archiving or suppressing never-activated accounts rather than deleting them
States that suppression keeps the active-rate metric honest and leaves the door open
Places the final-notice email far later than the proposed 60 days, at roughly six months of zero clicks and zero replies
Frames that final notice as housekeeping rather than punishment
Separates never-activated affiliates (never clicked) from dormant ones (were active, then stopped) and states they get different messages
Limits re-engagement to roughly one or two touches before the final notice
Puts a diagnostic checkpoint at the end of the activation window, before any re-engagement message is sent
Equips the re-engagement touch with one concrete incentive and one ready-to-use asset, not encouragement alone

evals.prompt: We sell an enterprise data-catalog platform, average sales cycle is about five months, ACV around $60k. We just opened a partner referral program - 18 approvals last month, a mix of boutique data consultancies and two systems integrators. I've got one partner manager who can do calls. I've written a 14-day welcome drip and I'm going to measure activation as 'first referral within 30 days of approval.' Sanity check my plan and fill in the gaps?
evals.expected_output: A correction of the 30-day window to roughly 90 days on B2B deal physics, a deep-funnel activation event associated to the partner in CRM, day-0 sandbox and deal-registration provisioning, a trigger layer stretched across the window, and hybrid/high-touch routing with a kickoff-call agenda.
expectations: Rejects the 30-day activation window for this program and recommends roughly 90 days instead
Ties that window to the stated five-month sales cycle rather than to a generic default
Requires the activation event to be pinned to one deep-funnel milestone (lead, trial, accepted demo, qualified opportunity, or closed-won) rather than left as 'first referral'
Requires the chosen conversion event to be recorded and associated to the partner in the CRM
Keeps a 4-6 touch, 10-14 day calendar skeleton but stretches the behavior-trigger layer across the full 90-day window
Names at least two B2B-appropriate behavior triggers, such as training or certification completed, or no deal registered by a given day
Requires sandbox, demo, or NFR access to be provisioned at approval rather than granted on request
Requires the deal-registration link to be available at day 0
Recommends a hybrid or high-touch tier as viable given roughly 18 approvals a month and a named partner manager with call capacity
Includes a kickoff-call agenda covering the concrete activation plan, a first-deal date, and next-step owners
Adds B2B-specific kit items such as competitor-comparison or buyer-question material, beyond logos, banners and swipe copy
Notes that recurring commission carries clawback or reversal risk on every invoice, so payout holds run longer than in B2C
Places the time-boxed activation nudge inside the 90-day window rather than at day 30

evals.prompt: Quick one. Our 30-day affiliate activation rate came in at 19% for the August cohort - B2C, fashion accessories. My head of growth pulled a number off a blog saying 30% is the industry standard and now wants to pause the program and go re-recruit better affiliates. Is 19% actually bad? What should I tell her, and what number should we be holding ourselves to going forward? Also our all-time activation rate across every affiliate we've ever approved is 11%, which looks worse - which one do I report?
evals.expected_output: A verdict that 19% sits at or above the ~18% median B2C gate, a correction that the 30% figure is a diagnostic trigger rather than a pass gate, an honest reliability label on all these vendor figures, a rejection of re-recruiting as the response, and a switch to monthly-cohort reporting.
expectations: States that 19% sits at or above the roughly 18% median 30-day B2C activation figure, so the cohort is not failing
Identifies the 30% figure as a diagnostic trigger for investigation, not a pass or ship gate
Notes that holding the program to roughly 30% on day one demands top-quartile performance
Labels the benchmark numbers as vendor or practitioner figures rather than audited studies
Gives the wider context that only roughly 5-20% of approved affiliates ever produce a tracked conversion
Rejects re-recruiting as the response and directs any diagnosis at the sequence itself (provisioning, first touch, nudge)
Recommends reporting by monthly approval cohort rather than the blended all-time rate
Explains that a blended all-time rate hides whether the sequence is improving
States that a cohort is judged only once its activation window has closed
Names time-to-first-conversion, tracked as a cohort median, as a KPI alongside activation rate
Names never-activated share of the cohort at the cutoff as a KPI
Does not present any benchmark figure as an industry standard the user can quote as established fact

evals.prompt: Setting up partner onboarding for Reyvant, we sell a clinical trial management suite. Our whole partner roster is 14 CROs and consultancies - we added 3 this quarter and expect maybe 6 more next year. Each one that lands a deal is worth north of $200k in first-year contract value. I have a partner manager with open calendar time. I was going to copy the onboarding drip our marketing team uses for trial signups: build out the automated email sequence, the portal, the self-serve asset library, the works. What should the sequence look like?
evals.expected_output: An inversion of the default tier ordering - high-touch as primary because near-zero volume makes the per-partner hour cheap and the drip's build never pays back - with a kickoff-call agenda, day-0 provisioning kept as a pre-condition, and the plan delivered as the SEQUENCE PLAN artifact.
expectations: Inverts the default tier ordering and recommends high-touch as the primary tier for this roster
Gives the reason as near-zero partner volume making the per-partner manager hour cheap while the self-serve drip's build never pays back
Declines to build the full automated drip, portal and self-serve asset library as the centerpiece of the plan
States explicitly that the default efficiency ordering (self-serve ahead of hybrid ahead of high-touch) is a default to re-rank against the program, not a rule
Notes that high-touch requires almost no upfront build but becomes a standing recurring job
Includes a kickoff-call agenda covering terms and commission recap, targets with a concrete activation plan and next-step owners, a product walkthrough with sandbox access, and a first-deal date
Keeps day-0 provisioning as a pre-condition: portal credentials, deal-registration link, and sandbox or NFR access at approval
Keeps terms and disclosure attestation, plus tax and payout collection gating payout eligibility, at onboarding
Keeps the one-action-per-touch rule even inside the high-touch plan
Defines the activation event and its window before laying out the touch plan
Delivers the plan in the SEQUENCE PLAN artifact format rather than as an undifferentiated list of emails

evals.prompt: Looking at our affiliate onboarding numbers. Touch 1 gets 61% opens and 28% clicks, touch 2 gets 54% opens, touch 3 gets 9% opens and almost no clicks, touch 4 and 5 are back around 40%. Touch 3 is the 'how do you plan to promote?' check-in and it goes out from our program@ address. I want to scrap the whole 5-email drip and replace it with a single onboarding hub page - recorded walkthrough video, all assets in one place, fully self-serve. Our dev team can get it built this quarter. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the hub swap because opens recover at touches 4 and 5, a copy-plane diagnosis of touch 3 pinned to the sender mismatch on a reply-seeking email, the trim-beats-hub ordering with its effort and reversibility numbers, and the condition under which a hub would actually be right.
expectations: Rejects replacing the full drip with a hub for this engagement pattern
Points out that opens recover at touches 4 and 5, so touch volume itself is not the friction
Diagnoses touch 3 as a copy-plane problem rather than a structural one
Identifies the sender mismatch: a touch asking for a reply is sent from an automated program address instead of a named person
States the ordering that trimming the drip beats swapping in a hub on activation bought per unit of build
Sizes the hub as roughly a few weeks of build plus a standing job to keep current, against roughly an hour to trim
Notes that reverting a hub means rebuilding the drip that was deleted, so the swap is far less reversible
States the condition under which the hub would be right: opens decaying across the whole sequence, not one touch underperforming
If a hub is adopted at all, keeps touch 1 and the behavior-trigger layer and collapses only the middle touches
Keeps the one-action, one-CTA rule for the rewritten touch 3
Does not recommend a rebuild before reading what the existing per-touch data already says

evals.prompt: I'm building the affiliate activation emails for Hoymar (B2C outdoor gear, 30-day window, 60-day cookie, coupon and content affiliates). My boss wants the sequence structured on AIDA so it maps to how the rest of our marketing is built, and he also forwarded a guide referencing something called the '60/40 principle' for affiliate onboarding that he wants applied. Can you build it out on those two?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to force-fit AIDA and a refusal to apply the unverified 60/40 principle, replaced by the day-offset skeleton plus behavior-trigger layer, with any named re-engagement framework labelled as one practitioner's coinage.
expectations: Declines to structure the sequence on AIDA and states that general marketing funnels are not built for affiliate activation
Declines to apply the '60/40 principle' and states it is unverified, with no named originator or citation behind it
Does not invent content or a definition for the 60/40 principle
Offers a day-offset skeleton plus a behavior-trigger layer as the structure instead
States the skeleton as roughly 4-6 touches over 10-14 days, each asking one action
Presents that skeleton as a defensible starting point rather than a fixed industry calendar
States that a behavior trigger overrides the calendar touch it collides with
If a named framework is used for the re-engagement branch, labels it as one practitioner's coinage rather than an industry-standard method
Keeps the activation window at 30 days and puts a deadline-bound nudge inside it
Does not present RACE, AARRR or AIDA as an accepted affiliate-onboarding framework

evals.prompt: Two messes in our affiliate onboarding automation at Bellfort (B2C kitchenware). First, people who already made a sale on day 3 keep getting the rest of the welcome drip, including the day-21 'make your first sale' bonus email - one of them replied 'do you people not see my orders?' Second, we're reactivating about 40 affiliates out of the archive next month for the holiday push and I don't know whether to drop them back at the top of the sequence. Oh, and a few affiliates are mid-thread with me over email while the automation keeps firing at them. How do I fix the flow control?
evals.expected_output: Flow-control rules: exit on activation with a celebration touch, re-entry at the tools touch rather than the welcome touch, suppression while a reply thread is open, a trigger-overrides-calendar rule, branch-entry exit, and an explicit flag on transactional-versus-marketing unsubscribe handling.
expectations: Exits an affiliate from the calendar sequence the moment the activation event tracks
Fires a distinct celebration touch on first sale and hands over to ongoing program communications
States that continuing the onboarding drip past activation reads as unattended automation
Has the first-sale celebration state when the commission approves and when it pays
Re-enters reactivated archived affiliates at the tools touch (T2), not at the welcome touch (T1)
Gives the reason that reactivated affiliates need a working asset and one action, not re-approval
Suppresses calendar touches while a reply thread with the affiliate manager is open
Specifies that entry into the never-activated branch ends the main sequence
Adds a trigger-overrides-calendar rule: when a behavior trigger fires within a day of a scheduled calendar touch, send the trigger touch and skip or delay the calendar one
Gives the reason that two emails in one day from the same program trains the skim reflex
Honors unsubscribes program-wide
Flags whether transactional notices (commission approved, payout sent) may still send after a marketing unsubscribe as a question for the program's terms and local law, rather than assuming they may

evals.prompt: I've got 19 days before our next affiliate cohort gets approved and I need to fix what I can before then. Known problems, all real: the tracking link sits below a 400-word block of brand guidelines in our welcome email; that same email also attaches the terms PDF, 14 banners and a certification invite; there's no follow-up at all for people who never click; we send one identical sequence to coupon sites, cashback sites and Instagram creators alike; and we've been paying commissions for four months without ever collecting a W-9 or payout details from anyone. No budget for design work and nobody to add to the team. What order do I do these in?
evals.expected_output: An explicit fix ordering by activation bought per hour, led by link placement then the welcome dump, with the tax and payout gap pulled out of that ordering onto a compliance clock, the routing-versus-branch tie broken by which window each pays in, and design work deleted rather than ranked last.
expectations: Puts moving the tracking link into the first lines of touch 1 first, as a near-zero-effort fix
Puts breaking up the welcome dump into one action per touch second
States the fix ordering as activation bought per hour of fixing, explicitly, not as an implied row order
Pulls the missing tax and payout collection out of that activation ordering entirely
Justifies that separation because it buys avoided payout disputes and reduced legal exposure rather than activation
Tells the user to fix the tax and payout gap on the compliance clock, before further commissions are earned, whatever the activation work is doing
Notes that commissions already earned against uncollected tax forms become a negotiation with the affiliate rather than a build task
Treats archetype routing and the never-activated branch as roughly equal on ratio, each a day or two of work
Breaks that tie on timing: routing pays inside the window the user is already in, while the never-activated branch only pays on the next cohort
Uses the 19-day deadline to promote the near-zero fixes and demote or drop anything requiring a build
Deletes the banner and design work from the list outright given the stated no-design-budget constraint, rather than ranking it last
Does not delay the cohort's launch until a complete asset kit exists

evals.prompt: Write me the actual welcome email for Norrsken Supply's affiliate program - B2C, we sell camping gear. 15% commission on the order total, 45-day cookie, $75 payout threshold, commissions approve after our 30-day return window closes and pay net-30. Links and codes are auto-generated at approval. The affiliate I'm writing to is a newsletter writer with about 20k subscribers. I want it to feel personal and I want them to reply to me - I'm Tomas, I run the program. Send it over and I'll paste it straight into our ESP.
evals.expected_output: A touch-1 email under 300 words with the link and code in the first lines, one action and one CTA, all money mechanics stated plainly, a concrete subject line, the named human as sender, disclosure and terms surfaced, and an explicit instruction that the draft goes through a humanizer pass before it is treated as final.
expectations: Places the tracking link and coupon code in the first lines of the email
Asks exactly one action, with one call to action
Keeps the email under roughly 300 words
Writes the call to action as action plus outcome rather than 'learn more' or equivalent
States the money mechanics plainly: the 15% commission, the 45-day cookie, the $75 payout threshold, approval after the 30-day return window, and net-30 payment
Sets the subject line on the concrete thing inside the email (the link or code) rather than on program excitement such as 'Welcome aboard'
Sends the email from Tomas by name rather than from an automated or no-reply program address
Notes that a reply-seeking email sent from a no-reply or automated address undercuts its own ask
Uses the affiliate's own archetype context, for example their subscribers or their newsletter, rather than the program's framing
Surfaces the disclosure obligation and terms acceptance in this first touch
States that the draft must go through a humanizer pass before it is treated as final copy, rather than handing over raw first-draft output as paste-ready
Specifies that the humanizer pass rewrites tone and phrasing only, leaving the one-action structure and the money mechanics unchanged
